### Founding Myths

According to Roman mythology, Rome was founded on April 21, 753 BCE, by Romulus and Remus, twin brothers who were abandoned as infants and suckled by a she-wolf (Livy, 1.1-1.7; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, 1.76-79). After a dispute, Romulus killed Remus and became the first king of Rome, naming the city after himself. While the historicity of this myth is debated among scholars, it remains an integral part of Roman identity and cultural heritage (Beard, 2015, p. 27).

The early history of Rome is shrouded in legend, but archaeological evidence suggests that the city was inhabited from around the 8th century BCE (Cornell, 1995, p. 57). The Roman Kingdom, which lasted from approximately 753 BCE to 509 BCE, was a period of monarchical rule with seven kings, the last of whom, Lucius Tarquinius Superbus, was overthrown in a revolution that established the Roman Republic (Livy, 1.46-60).

### The Republic Period

The Roman Republic (509-27 BCE) was characterized by a complex system of governance, with power divided among the Senate, the Assemblies, and various magistrates (Cicero, De Republica, 2.23-30). This period saw Rome expand from a city-state to a dominant power in the Mediterranean. Key events include the conquest of Italy, the Punic Wars against Carthage (264-146 BCE), and the incorporation of Greece and other territories into the Roman sphere (Polybius, 1.1-6; Livy, 21-30).

The Republic was marked by significant social and political tensions, including the struggle between the patrician (noble) class and the plebeians (commoners), which led to important reforms such as the creation of the tribunate and the publication of the Twelve Tables (Livy, 3.31-55; Cicero, De Republica, 2.53-61). Augustus established the Principate, a system of government in which the emperor held supreme power but was also responsible for the welfare of the Roman people (Tacitus, Annals, 1.1-6).

### Major Emperors

The Roman Empire was ruled by a succession of emperors, some of whom left lasting legacies. Augustus' reign (27 BCE-14 CE) is often considered the "Golden Age" of Rome, characterized by relative peace (the Pax Romana), administrative reforms, and cultural achievements (Suetonius, Augustus, 28-40; Tacitus, Annals, 1.1-6). The decline of the Roman Empire is a complex and multifaceted process that has been the subject of much debate among historians (Gibbon, 1776-1789; Heather, 2005). Factors contributing to the decline include external pressures from barbarian tribes, internal corruption and instability, economic troubles, and military overextension (Heather, 2005, pp. 45-67).
